query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a rapidly solidified, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with density below 6 g/cm³, the partial decomposition of its metastable, magnesium-rich solid solutions into stable intermetallic phases during thermal exposure drives local compositional redistribution, which modifies passivation behavior and alters both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation. Specifically, the enrichment of magnesium in newly formed intermetallic phases leads to the depletion of protective elements (e.g., Al) in the matrix and changes in oxide scale composition, resulting in a measurable shift—either improving or degrading—of the alloy’s corrosion and oxidation performance relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: Non-equilibrium as-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (e.g., induction-melted Al–Mg–rich multi-principal system) with metastable solid solutions.
generation.intervention: Systematic thermal exposures at incrementally higher temperatures (e.g., 200–700 °C) to induce controlled phase decomposition, followed by immersion in corrosive media or exposure to oxidative environments at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Identical alloy composition and preparation route until post-casting heat treatments that vary in temperature and duration, accompanied by standardized electrochemical corrosion tests and thermogravimetric oxidation measurements at up to 700 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation of metastable Mg-containing solid solutions into stable intermetallic compounds, with corresponding changes in local composition and interface morphologies.
generation.mechanism: Decomposition of Mg-rich metastable phases releases or partitions Mg and other solutes, altering both the microstructural pathways for oxide scale formation at high temperature and the extents of passivation or pitting in corrosive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with as-cast baseline samples, thermally exposed specimens will exhibit measurable differences in both corrosion potential/current density and oxidation mass gain at high temperature, consistent with distinct stable intermetallic formation and changed oxide or passivation behavior.
generation.baseline: The as-cast alloy’s corrosion resistance and oxide formation kinetics before heat treatment, which are characteristic of Mg-rich metastable solid solutions and limited stable intermetallic formation.
generation.boundary: At temperatures or durations insufficient to decompose the metastable Mg-rich phases, corrosion and oxidation behaviors should not deviate significantly from the as-cast baseline. Extremely high temperatures or prolonged aging may lead to complete phase transformation and could produce new behavior dominated by stable intermetallics.
generation.uncertainty: Exact composition-dependent transformation rates and the net effect on corrosion or oxidation (improvement vs. degradation) may vary across different Mg and alloying element contents, requiring further experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare alloy ingots via induction melting with nominal aluminum, magnesium, and additional multi-principal elements. Rapidly solidify and then subject separate specimens to stepwise 200–700 °C heat treatments while holding for different durations. After each step or hold time, measure mass changes upon oxidation and evaluate corrosion performance in an electrolyte, comparing to an as-cast control group.
measurements: Phase identification via in situ diffraction (e.g., XRD) and TEM to track metastable-to-stable transformations.
Quantitative EDS mapping to detect local changes in elemental distribution in matrix vs. new intermetallic phases.
Potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy for corrosion resistance.
Thermogravimetric analysis and post-oxidation microstructure characterization (SEM/EDS).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If extended thermal exposure results in no distinct phase transformations or if corrosion and oxidation responses remain identical to the as-cast control, then the hypothesized link between metastable-to-stable phase decomposition and altered environmental resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,].
